Non-tree cultivation areas include areas with small and large scale agricultural crops. Prairie is a type of vegetation cover that settles in plains dominated by grass and shrubs or woods (tree prairie) and scrub (semi-always green and semi deciduous) with less than 30% tree cover. These formations occupy regions with annual rainfall below 1200 mm. In these formations the acacias predominate;Acacia nigrescensens, Acacia xantophloea, A. nilotica, A. goetzei, which, in some cases, are associated with other xerophilic species such as Commiphora spp.

Wetlands comprise areas permanently or temporarily flooded with or without shrub or herbaceous vegetation. In the present classification this class was defined up to the second classification level, incorporating shrub vegetation, wetland and water body. In these areas there are marshy places, marshes, peat or water, natural or artificial, permanent or temporary, with stagnant or running water, fresh or brackish.

Mangroves are intertidal forests in tropical and sub-tropical zones, occupying sheltered coasts and places with little influence of tidal energy. Just over 70 species of mangroves are recognized globally, including true mangroves (about 42 species) and associated species (about 32 species). In Mozambique, this type of training consists of essentially by the following species: Avicennia marina (white mangrove), Bruguiera gymnhoriza (red mango), Tagal ceriops (white mangrove), Coastal Heritiera (Mozambique mangrove), Lumnitzera racemosa (black sleeve), Rhizophora mucronata (red mangrove), Alba Sonneracy (mangrove apple) and Xylocarpus granatum (cannon ball mangal).

Mecrusse is a type of vegetation that occurs in Mozambique in a gregarious way, where the main species present in its canopy is Androstachys johnsonii, belongs to the Euphorbiaceae family. This vegetation is characterized by low biological diversity and uniformity in terms of individuals, both in diameter and in height. In Mozambique it is found in Gaza, Inhambane and small patches in Nampula province.

The mountain forest ranges from 1200 to 1600 m in altitude with rainfall from 1,700 to 2000 mm per year or in places where there is a sudden change in altitude (300 to 2500 m). These forests occur in the regions of Chimanimani (Moribane), Gurué, Milange, Vumba, Gorongosa, Namuli, Tamassa, Mueda plateau and among other highlands. The transition from low-altitude forests to Mountain forests occurs continuously, with a progressive replacement of species and the determining factor for the site is the high air humidity. In terms of composition, these forests have a lower specific diversity compared to those at low altitude. Typical species are:Widdringtonia whytei, Acacia abyssinica subsp, calophylla, Podocarpus spp., Celtis gomphophylla, Maesa lanceolata, Tabernaemontana stapfian, Curtisia dentata, Macaranga spp, Bombax rhodognaphalon, Diospyros mespiliformis, Cussonia spicata, Milicia excelsa, Cordyla africana, Kigelia africana, Newtonia buchananii, Ficus spp., Uapaca spp.,Vitex spp.
